description: UDEM ITC students. We like to code and build useful things.
summary: Xopan is a web app that helps rainfed farmers in Nuevo León, Mexico, explore what to plant after sorghum. Farmers can outline a field on a satellite map or open a sample field near Linares. The app brings together NASA climate and satellite data, local soil mapping from INEGI, and information about three crop options: grain sorghum again, dry beans, or forage sorghum. Farmers can compare a typical rainfall year with a dry year and change how much they value income, water saving, and soil health. Xopan explains why the options are ranked in that order and what to check locally before choosing a rotation. The ranking uses team estimates, while the environmental data help farmers understand the risks behind their decision.
details:
How it works. A farmer outlines a field or opens the sample field near Linares, Nuevo León. Xopan shows map layers for rainfall, air temperature, vegetation greenness, soil moisture, and soil water retention. The field report compares two historical scenarios. At the sample location, NASA POWER estimates 711 mm of rain in the typical year and 623 mm in the dry year. The INEGI soil map indicates clayey topsoil in the area, giving the farmer a practical question to check: does water collect on the field after rain?

How the comparison works. The farmer sets priorities for income, water saving, and soil health. Xopan uses those priorities to weight the team's ratings and shows the calculation behind each position. Climate and soil data help the farmer interpret risks; they do not change the score. Irrigation availability changes the advice shown in the report.

What makes it useful. Xopan puts the map, historical evidence, and crop trade-offs in one place. The pilot focuses on three options after sorghum so farmers can see what to explore first and what they still need to verify. Our next step is to test the workflow with producers and expand the catalog using locally validated crop information.

Technology. We built the web app with Next.js, React, JavaScript, and the Google Maps JavaScript API. We used Python to prepare geospatial datasets and Vercel to host the prototype. Source code: https://github.com/Gael-sanchez-ramos/Nasa-2026-field-shift
